prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties of 10^-18 and opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest example on the shortlist of a measurement advance that changes what can be observed. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem, and the first strontium lattice clock showed the principle experimentally. Ye's group then demonstrated spin-polarised fermion operation, control of collisional and blackbody systematics, and long coherence, which brought the uncertainty to the 10^-18 level. Several independent laboratories now reproduce that performance and compare clocks, so this is not a single-lab claim. The consequences are concrete: millimetre- and centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, constraints on varying constants and dark matter, relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. This matches my own view that our knowledge is limited by what we can measure and how precisely. A Katori and Ye prize is a clean two-person attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is that optical clocks and frequency combs have already been recognised (2005, 2012), so the committee may see 10^-18 lattice clocks as a very impressive refinement rather than a new discovery. Other groups (ion clocks, ytterbium lattice clocks at NIST, PTB and SYRTE) also drove the performance, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest application is still ahead. From my own experience with coherence-limited systems, I also know that the road from record uncertainty to broad scientific use is long, and I cannot claim the new-physics payoff has been demonstrated yet.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the defect-mediated 2D melting theory (B006) first and the lattice clocks second, valuing simple general mechanisms, and asks whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition.
responses.response: I agree that the magic-wavelength idea is simple and general, and that is part of why I rank clocks first. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree: the scientific result, 10^-18 uncertainty reproduced and compared across labs, is already established, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from it rather than validates it. Waiting would reward a bureaucratic milestone, not the physics. On B006 I respect the elegance, but you note yourself that you recall the history from memory and that some 2D melting transitions are first order. As an experimentalist I would want the decisive experimental evidence for the hexatic phase to be firmer, and the Kosterlitz-Thouless overlap with 2016 is large, so I do not put it ahead of a result with this much direct measurement behind it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance (B015) first for its original experiments and enormous technological deployment, and ranks clocks second, asking whether they are only a refinement of earlier clock and comb prizes.
responses.response: B015 is a serious candidate, and I accept that an original 1995 experimental discovery with thirty years of confirmation and industrial uptake has a strong claim; my hesitation is mostly attribution, because the Moodera, Miyazaki and Parkin priority question and the later MgO step, with Yuasa and the Butler and Mathon theory, make the three-name credit hard to defend. On the refinement worry: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb and the 2012 prize rewarded single-quantum-system control with ion clocks. The lattice clock is a different principle, a many-atom system with interactions and lattice light shifts engineered to cancel, and a reduction in uncertainty by about two orders of magnitude over the best ion clocks, which opened gravitational-redshift and dark-matter applications that earlier clocks could not reach. I see that as a new capability, not a polish.

responses.point: Pearce ranks clocks first for a clear explainable consequence (a centimetre height difference seen by a clock) but wants the redefinition of the second to be well advanced, and ranks the Higgs detector conception (B002) second.
responses.response: I share your reading of the clock result and think the centimetre-redshift demonstration is exactly the kind of explainable consequence the citation can lean on. On B002 I would qualify strongly: ATLAS and CMS are extraordinary instruments, and I have no doubt about the measurement quality, but the prize would honour three conceivers or spokespersons for work done by thousands, and you yourself note that discovery-year spokespersons, analysis leaders and accelerator builders are excluded. A prize for the discovery would be easier to defend scientifically than one for detector conception, so I would put B002 behind the clocks and also behind candidates where attribution is cleaner. I would also push back mildly on your wish for the redefinition to be well advanced; the physics is mature now.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks clocks first, but gives B042 (ultracold atoms in optical lattices) second and circuit QED (B003) fifth, noting that the 2025 circuit prize makes B003 a natural follow-up but possibly too close.
responses.response: I agree on the top candidate. On B042, I rank it third and see it as the main alternative: quantum simulation with optical lattices is well reproduced and widely used, but the five-name credit exceeds three laureates and the choice among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Esslinger is the difficulty. For B003 I rank it fourth and am more cautious than your phrase 'natural follow-up' suggests. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close enough that awarding circuit QED immediately risks looking repetitive, and the theory credit among Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is also split. I would hold both as alternatives, not as co-equal parts of a shared prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as a new discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
Whether other clock groups (ytterbium lattice, ion clocks at NIST and PTB) have claims strong enough to displace or join Katori and Ye.
How much weight the pending SI second redefinition should carry in timing the award.
Whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would improve the configuration or only dilute it, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I note only general field proximity: I work in atomic physics and quantum optics (Lund) and have collaborated broadly in quantum memories, but I have no mentor, co-author or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names that I know of. My WACQT role at Chalmers overlaps with Göran Johansson's institution, which matters only for superconducting-circuit candidates such as B003.
